sections.heading: When a child’s first language became a school offence
paragraphs: Welsh did not become less secure because its speakers suddenly stopped caring. English gained authority in education and public advancement, while institutions often treated Welsh as an obstacle. The 1847 education inquiry intensified that stigma: three commissioners who did not speak Welsh made disparaging judgments about the language, religion, and morality of the people they assessed.

The Welsh Not makes that history tangible. Museum Wales documents its use at Maestir School: children caught speaking Welsh wore a wooden token, pupils were encouraged to report one another, and the child holding it at day’s end was caned. This is documented punishment, not a metaphor. Its use varied; it should not be presented as a single law imposed identically in every Welsh school.

sections.heading: A language kept alive, then fought for in public
paragraphs: The Blue Books provoked an immediate and lasting reaction, becoming known as Brad y Llyfrau Gleision—the Treachery of the Blue Books. The National Library of Wales connects their influence with the idea that advancement required English. Recognising that pressure helps explain language shift without blaming families who wanted education and opportunities for their children.

Welsh nevertheless continued in homes, communities, publishing, worship, and cultural life. Its modern story is therefore one of survival as well as revival. The 1967 and 1993 Welsh Language Acts, followed by the Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011, mark changing public rights. These milestones did not erase the earlier humiliation or automatically make every public encounter available in Welsh.

sections.heading: Recognition is not the same as a secure future
paragraphs: Welsh-medium education, public services, broadcasting, and community activity create places where Cymraeg can be more than a school subject. The distinction matters: being able to speak a language and having regular opportunities to use it are different things. A language can gain institutional visibility while still facing difficulty in the daily lives of its speakers.

The 2021 Census reported 538,300 Welsh speakers aged three and over in Wales, or 17.8 percent. This was lower than the 2011 proportion. Welsh Government treats the census as the principal benchmark for its million-speaker ambition, while survey estimates use different methods. A responsible revival story acknowledges that setback instead of declaring victory because Welsh appears on signs.

sections.heading: Type with care, then find a reason to use the language
paragraphs: For keyboard practice, preserve accents such as ŵ and ŷ and follow the source passage exactly. Welsh letter combinations including ll and dd are meaningful parts of its spelling system. A typing exercise should help you become comfortable producing the text, while pronunciation and meaning need attention of their own through suitable learning materials and speakers.

Begin with short passages whose spelling and provenance you can check. Read them before starting, keep unfamiliar words for later study, and measure improvement under comparable conditions. WPMTest contributes a place to practise writing; it does not certify Welsh fluency, represent Welsh-speaking communities, or replace the schools, families, teachers, and campaigners doing the long-term work.

sections.heading: Language shift without a single convenient ban date
paragraphs: Manx, or Gaelg, is the Gaelic language of the Isle of Man. Its decline was not a simple story of one prohibition followed by one rescue. Culture Vannin describes rapid social, economic, and population change in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Growing towns, trade, tourism, and English influence altered the settings in which people worked and raised their children.

As English became dominant, ordinary opportunities to acquire and use Manx narrowed. Within a few generations, English alone had become usual for much of the population. This account should not be softened into an entirely voluntary change, but neither should an editor invent a nationwide ban or a punishment system without the evidence to support it. Different languages experienced different mechanisms of loss.

sections.heading: Why the “last speaker” is not the end of the story
paragraphs: Ned Maddrell, widely described as the last traditional native speaker, died in 1974. The phrase is important but incomplete. Learners, collectors, teachers, and advocates had already begun sustaining Manx before his death. Describing the language as simply dead in that year erases the people who continued speaking, teaching, and creating material in it.

Yn Cheshaght Ghailckagh, the Manx Language Society, stresses that revival preceded Maddrell’s death. Recordings of traditional speakers, dictionaries, teaching, and community commitment helped later generations gain access. They did not remove every difficulty of rebuilding transmission. They provided material and relationships through which people could make Manx part of their own lives rather than merely a subject in a museum.

sections.heading: From learners’ commitment to children’s education
paragraphs: Manx entered schools in 1992. In 2001, Bunscoill Ghaelgagh opened, providing education through Manx rather than only an occasional lesson about it. The Language Society credits a parents’ campaign coordinated by Mooinjer Veggey. That difference matters: a language becomes a medium for learning and friendship when children have reasons to use it throughout the school day.

The 2022–2032 Manx Language Strategy brings together government, Manx National Heritage, Culture Vannin, and Mooinjer Veggey through the Jeebin network. Its ambitions include resources, training, advocacy, and education. A strategy expresses a commitment and a target; it is not evidence that the target has already been achieved. Continuing community use remains essential alongside formal plans.

sections.heading: Learning from Manx without treating it as a curiosity
paragraphs: Manx is related to Irish and Scottish Gaelic, but a practice passage must use Manx spelling and forms. Replacing an unfamiliar word with one from a related language changes the material. Use a named learning source, listen alongside reading where possible, and preserve the passage’s punctuation and spelling rather than relying on an English autocorrect system.

A keyboard exercise can make written Manx feel less unfamiliar. It cannot recreate the social environment that makes a language secure, test a learner’s pronunciation, or confer cultural authority. Follow community resources, attend learning opportunities when available, and treat speaker knowledge as more than a source of text. The purpose is to make room for use, not to announce that outsiders have saved the language.

sections.heading: Schooling that made Gaelic smaller
paragraphs: Gaelic decline cannot be understood through a single event. Political marginalisation, economic pressure, displacement, migration, and English-dominant institutions all affected its transmission. Education is a particularly clear part of that history. The Education (Scotland) Act 1872 established compulsory state schooling without providing for Gaelic, reinforcing an education system that was already becoming increasingly anglicised.

The consequences went beyond a missing subject on a timetable. Archival and educational accounts document children being punished for speaking Gaelic. Such practices taught children that their home language could bring humiliation in the institution responsible for their advancement. The law did not itself contain one simple clause ordering every punishment; the distinction between legislative exclusion and classroom enforcement matters.

sections.heading: The long work of restoring a place in education
paragraphs: When a language loses space in school, the damage can follow children home. Families making decisions under unequal conditions may shift toward the language associated with qualifications or work. That is not proof that they valued Gaelic less. A truthful account recognises the pressure while avoiding a claim that all communities experienced the same sequence or degree of loss.

Gaelic-medium education is part of the response: Gaelic becomes the language through which children learn, rather than being confined to a vocabulary exercise. Bòrd na Gàidhlig’s statutory guidance addresses education authorities, parents, and other public bodies. It recognises that supporting a language requires structures and responsibilities, not simply praise for its cultural importance.

sections.heading: From the 2005 framework to the 2025 Act
paragraphs: The Gaelic Language (Scotland) Act 2005 established Bòrd na Gàidhlig as a statutory body, created a framework for language plans, and provided for guidance on Gaelic education. The Act commenced in February 2006. It was a major institutional change, but legal recognition should not be confused with the restoration of all the community settings weakened over generations.

The Scottish Languages Act 2025 subsequently provided explicit official status for Gaelic and Scots. The relevant official-status provisions took effect on 30 November 2025. This is an important development beyond the earlier 2005 account. It creates further duties and policy tools, while leaving the practical work of education, community use, publishing, and everyday transmission to be carried forward.

sections.heading: Respect the written language and the people using it
paragraphs: For typing, retain grave accents such as à, è, ì, ò, and ù. Scottish Gaelic and Irish are distinct languages despite their relationship. Choose material with an identifiable source, follow its orthographic conventions, and do not silently substitute forms from another Gaelic language. Familiarity with a keyboard is only one small part of learning to understand and use the words.

A useful practice session is short enough to check carefully and supported by meaning or audio where available. Compare your own results using comparable passages and devices. WPM is a mechanical measure, not a score for belonging, intelligence, or fluency. Supporting Gaelic also means listening to community priorities and recognising that an online tool’s role is limited beside the work of speakers, families, teachers, and organisations.

sections.heading: Loss under unequal power, not lack of attachment
paragraphs: Irish, or Gaeilge, was weakened by centuries of political and social change under English rule. The decline of institutions supporting Irish, the advantages attached to English, and changes in schooling affected how families could use and transmit the language. This was not one moment when an entire population freely chose to abandon its words.

The Great Famine of 1845–1852 brought catastrophic death, suffering, and migration. Language transmission cannot be separated from the communities that carry it. Famine and emigration damaged the social setting in which Irish was used, particularly in already vulnerable communities. Reducing that history to a cheerful story of a language becoming fashionable again would conceal the scale of the human loss.

sections.heading: Revival meant building public space for Irish
paragraphs: Conradh na Gaeilge, the Gaelic League, was founded in 1893. Its work connected language learning with public respect for Irish at a time when the language had no official recognition. Classes and branches created opportunities for people to learn and use it, while publishing helped expand the settings in which written Irish could appear.

This was not simply the recovery of an old text. The movement supported a living language and the people who spoke it. Library and cultural accounts describe teaching native speakers to read and write in Irish as well as teaching learners. That distinction challenges the assumption that literacy in English was the only useful form of education available to Irish-speaking communities.

sections.heading: Official recognition and everyday use remain different questions
paragraphs: Irish received constitutional recognition in the independent state, including its position as the first official language in the 1937 Constitution. Later official-language legislation addressed public services. These changes are significant, but they do not mean every person who studies Irish can use it comfortably or that Irish-speaking communities no longer face pressure.

Gaeltacht communities, Irish-medium education, broadcasting, publishing, and organisations such as Conradh na Gaeilge sustain distinct parts of the language’s public and community life. Learners matter, and so do settings where Irish is already spoken. Supporting revival means strengthening the circumstances of use, rather than treating official status or the availability of a course as proof that transmission has become secure.

sections.heading: Let careful practice lead to understanding
paragraphs: Keep the síneadh fada in words that require it: á, é, í, ó, and ú. Follow the passage’s spelling, initial mutations, punctuation, and spacing. An English keyboard’s autocorrect can introduce errors that are easy to miss. Set up a suitable input method and check a short sample before beginning a timed exercise.

WPMTest offers keyboard practice, not a certificate of Irish fluency or a substitute for instruction from competent speakers. Read a passage for meaning before copying it, and use trusted audio or teaching material to connect the written words with speech. A higher score is useful only for the task measured. The larger purpose is to become more able and willing to use Irish in appropriate everyday settings.

sections.heading: Where is Catalan spoken?
paragraphs: Catalan is a language, not the name of a country. Catalonia (Catalunya), whose capital is Barcelona, is an autonomous community in northeastern Spain. Catalan is also spoken in the Valencian Community, where it is called Valencian, and the Balearic Islands; in Andorra, an independent country; in Northern Catalonia in southern France; and in Alghero on the Italian island of Sardinia. Smaller traditional Catalan-speaking areas include eastern Aragon and El Carche in Murcia, Spain. These communities span four countries: Spain, Andorra, France, and Italy.

sections.heading: Public repression did not begin with a lack of speakers
paragraphs: Catalan is a living language with a substantial literary, educational, and community presence. Its inclusion here concerns a history of repression and the work of maintaining public use, not a claim that it is nearly extinct. Catalan-speaking territories also have different political and legal histories; Catalonia’s experience cannot stand for every speaker.

After the Spanish Civil War, Franco’s dictatorship subjected Catalan to systematic persecution, particularly in the 1940s and 1950s. The Generalitat’s history describes restrictions on education, publishing, and other public communication. Removing a language from those settings affects more than visibility: it narrows the opportunities through which children encounter it as a language of knowledge, authority, and ordinary adult life.

sections.heading: Culture continued under conditions it did not choose
paragraphs: The dictatorship also dismantled Catalan political institutions. An account of the language must therefore consider the wider loss of public authority and cultural freedom. It would be misleading to present the period as merely a temporary decline in interest in Catalan. Restrictions were imposed, and people who maintained cultural activity did so within unequal and changing conditions.

The existence of cultural resistance does not make the repression less serious. Nor should the entire dictatorship be described as though every restriction operated identically in every year. Institutional and scholarly histories document both coercion and continued cultural activity. Keeping those facts together gives a more honest account than either a simple disappearance narrative or an uncomplicated story of heroic recovery.

sections.heading: Rebuilding rights, education, and opportunities to speak
paragraphs: After Franco’s death in 1975, democratic change opened a different legal setting. The 1978 Constitution recognised linguistic plurality; the 1979 Statute restored co-official recognition in Catalonia. Language policy and cultural institutions then worked to extend Catalan’s use. Legal milestones matter because they change what institutions may support, but they do not remove every pressure affecting daily choices.

The Consortium for Language Normalisation provides adult courses and works to broaden knowledge and social use. Voluntariat per la llengua connects learners with fluent speakers for conversation. These are practical examples of making a language usable outside a textbook. Terminology work, publishing, education, and community activity also help Catalan function across different parts of contemporary life.

sections.heading: Accents, regional forms, and the limits of a typing score
paragraphs: For typing, retain ç, the required accents and diaereses, and the middle dot in l·l. Follow the regional standard and conventions identified by the source. Respect Valencian naming and forms rather than treating variation as a mistake. A good exercise should tell you what text you are reproducing instead of silently combining material from incompatible conventions.

Use a short, checkable passage and read it for meaning before starting the timer. If a character is difficult to enter, practise the input method first. WPMTest measures copying performance; it cannot certify Catalan fluency or represent the priorities of Catalan-speaking communities. Pair keyboard familiarity with listening, conversation, reading, and resources created by speakers so the practice connects with a language people actually use.

sections.heading: When a familiar language is pushed out of public life
paragraphs: Taiwanese Taigi is not Mandarin with a different accent. It has its own spoken forms and writing traditions. Calling everything on this page simply Chinese would hide the very distinction that makes language transmission difficult: a child can become highly literate in Mandarin while losing opportunities to speak, read, or write Taigi.

After 1945, the Nationalist government promoted Mandarin as the sole national language. Taiwan’s Ministry of Education describes that period within a history of authoritarian education. These policies gave Mandarin institutional authority while reducing the public space available to other languages. That history should not be softened into a story of families simply choosing a more convenient language.

sections.heading: From linguistic hierarchy toward recognition
paragraphs: Changing the legal framework took decades. Local-language education entered school curricula, and the Development of National Languages Act was promulgated in January 2019. It recognized Taiwan’s natural languages and Taiwan Sign Language as national languages and established responsibilities for preservation, teaching, and support where transmission is at risk.

Recognition is meaningful, but it is not a report card proving that transmission has recovered. A language needs teachers, learning materials, public visibility, and people who can use it together. We therefore distinguish the date of a law from evidence about its effects, rather than presenting official recognition as the moment the problem was solved.

sections.heading: Revitalization includes the tools people actually use
paragraphs: Taiwan’s 2022–2026 national languages plan includes teacher preparation, digital resources, language corpora, media, and input tools. Its publication identifies Taigi among the languages for which materials are being collected. The Ministry of Education also provides a dictionary of frequently used Taiwanese Taigi, giving learners a route to check forms instead of guessing.

For a learner, these resources work best as a connection to listening and conversation. Read a short passage, hear it spoken, and ask what its expressions mean in context. A successful keyboard exercise can help someone reproduce a written form; it cannot by itself restore the conversational relationships through which a language is passed on.

sections.heading: Choose the writing system before starting the timer
paragraphs: Taigi materials may use Chinese characters, romanization, or a combination. Pe̍h-ōe-jī and Tâi-lô must be identified rather than silently mixed. Our publication standard is to name the convention, preserve tone marks and spelling, and obtain competent review before treating a passage as scored language material. A Mandarin sentence is not a substitute.

Check the input method and practice an untimed copy first. A missing tone mark, an altered combining mark, or a keyboard workaround can produce a mismatch even when the reader recognizes the word. Speed should come after accurate reproduction. Compare attempts using the same script and assistance settings; five-character WPM is not a measure of Taigi fluency.

sections.heading: Hakka belongs in public life as well as at home
paragraphs: Hakka’s reduced public space in Taiwan was not simply a matter of changing tastes. Mandarin-dominant institutions and broadcast restrictions made other languages less available and less authoritative. The Hakka Restoration Movement challenged that hierarchy. On December 28, 1988, demonstrators called for language equality and the right to hear and use Hakka publicly.

The demand was about more than preserving a sound archive. A language can remain meaningful to grandparents while children rarely encounter it in education, entertainment, or public services. The movement’s history helps explain why broadcasting, teaching, and ordinary public use became linked goals: household effort alone cannot compensate for institutions that privilege another language.

sections.heading: Sixian is a specific community pathway
paragraphs: The Hakka Affairs Council describes Sixian as widely used in Miaoli, southern Hakka settlements, and parts of Taoyuan. It also notes Sixian’s use in transport announcements. That visibility is valuable, but it should not make Sixian the unmarked substitute for every Hakka speaker’s language. Southern Sixian is also distinguished in the Taiwan Hakka Corpus.

A Sixian learner should ask which regional form a recording or passage follows. The same broad label does not eliminate local variation. A useful exercise pairs the text with an identified speaker or reliable reference, so learners can relate the spelling to a voice instead of treating a familiar-looking character as a complete pronunciation guide.

sections.heading: Rights need teaching, media, and usable materials
paragraphs: The Hakka Basic Act was promulgated in 2010 and revised in 2018. The revised framework affirms Hakka’s national-language status and supports public use, education, research, and communication. Those legal milestones represent a substantial change in institutional direction. They should not be mistaken for evidence that every child now receives sustained Hakka-medium education.

The Taiwan Hakka Corpus preserves written and spoken materials in multiple varieties, including Sixian and Southern Sixian. The Council describes a process involving native speakers and linguists in transcription and revision. That labor matters: recordings, accurate text, and clear labels create a resource learners can return to, beyond a single symbolic celebration.

sections.heading: Respect the variety when practicing on a keyboard
paragraphs: For Sixian practice, identify the regional form and writing system before selecting text. Do not interchange Sixian and Hailu spellings or tone notation simply to make a passage easier to type. When a dictionary offers multiple pronunciations, choose the intended variety explicitly and retain the source’s distinctions throughout the exercise.

Begin with a short untimed passage and check its meaning with a teacher or trusted recording. A typing result reports reproduction of the displayed text under particular input settings. It does not certify pronunciation, comprehension, cultural identity, or language proficiency. The useful goal is to make writing feel more available while continuing to listen, speak, and learn with people.

sections.heading: Hailu is a specific community pathway
paragraphs: The Hakka Affairs Council locates Hailu especially in the Hsinchu region, with communities in parts of Taoyuan, Miaoli, and Hualien. Hailu is therefore a specific learning pathway, not a decorative alternative name for Sixian. Its geographic description provides a useful starting point, without implying that every family in those places speaks the same way.

For Hailu, keeping the variety visible prevents a common digital shortcut: recycling the more easily obtained material of a neighboring variety. A text collection should identify the intended pronunciation and tone conventions. The reviewer’s competence must match Hailu, rather than relying on a general statement that a resource has been checked by a Hakka speaker.

sections.heading: Rights need teaching, media, and usable materials
paragraphs: The Hakka Basic Act was promulgated in 2010 and revised in 2018. The revised framework affirms Hakka’s national-language status and supports public use, education, research, and communication. Those legal milestones represent a substantial change in institutional direction. They should not be mistaken for evidence that every child now receives sustained Hakka-medium education.

The Taiwan Hakka Corpus includes Hailu among its separately identified varieties. Its collection draws on sources such as oral histories, interviews, daily conversation, and published or broadcast material, with transcription and revision by speakers and linguists. These are practical foundations for learning Hailu as a living voice, not merely recognizing Hakka as a cultural label.

sections.heading: Respect the variety when practicing on a keyboard
paragraphs: For Hailu practice, identify the writing system and tone convention explicitly. Material prepared for Sixian must not be relabeled Hailu without competent review. Where a reference offers several pronunciations, confirm that the chosen entry is the one intended. A browser’s ability to display a word does not establish that its language label is accurate.

sections.heading: A living language deserves a precise account of pressure
paragraphs: Wenzhounese connects people in Wenzhou and communities abroad. A responsible history must distinguish reduced transmission, institutional language hierarchies, migration, and direct legal prohibition. These processes can overlap, but they are not interchangeable. This article does not invent a single date when Wenzhounese was banned, or claim a verified worldwide speaker total.

For this collection, the strongest specific evidence comes from language-contact research rather than a simple suppression-and-rescue narrative. That distinction is important. A dramatic account of a lost language might attract attention, but it would make it harder to understand the actual choices families face when children grow up with several languages and uneven opportunities to use each one.

sections.heading: What a generational study can—and cannot—show
paragraphs: A 2020 study by Aalberse, Andringa, Faber, and Lippe compared two generations of Wenzhounese speakers in China and the Netherlands. It examined how speakers expressed definiteness, including classifier and demonstrative constructions. The researchers found generational effects, but not location effects in the phenomena they studied. That is a narrower finding than a claim about all aspects of the language.

The authors caution that changes among heritage speakers need not arise only from the overseas setting. Broader contact effects or internal change may also be involved, while Wenzhounese in China faces pressures of its own. This research does not justify describing younger speakers as speaking badly, or treating the speech of one location as an untouched standard.

sections.heading: Transmission begins with people, not a dramatic label
paragraphs: A useful response is to make space for the language in specific relationships. Ask relatives which local forms they use, record a story with permission, and learn the context of expressions that do not translate neatly. These are suggestions for respectful engagement, not evidence that one family practice can reverse a wider shift or substitute for organized community work.

Documentation and teaching materials should name their speakers, locality, and intended audience wherever consent and publication rules allow. A recording from one community should not be marketed as the single authentic voice of all Wenzhounese speakers. Preserving local differences can be more honest and more useful than forcing every resource into a uniform learning product.

sections.heading: Why a scored corpus needs more than Chinese characters
paragraphs: For this project, Wenzhounese passages require an explicitly declared writing convention and competent language review. A sentence written in Chinese characters does not automatically become Wenzhounese material, and a Mandarin passage must not be relabeled to fill a directory. If romanization is used, its notation must be explained and applied consistently rather than assembled from unrelated resources.

An untimed text-and-audio exercise is a better starting point when the writing conventions remain unfamiliar. Check meaning, punctuation, pronunciation references, and input behavior before comparing typing speed. A mechanically exact copy demonstrates copying under those conditions; it does not prove conversational ability. Until these publication requirements are met, an honestly labeled planned test is preferable to a misleading live one.

sections.heading: Sorani needs a regional history, not a borrowed ban date
paragraphs: Sorani, commonly called Central Kurdish, has a substantial written and literary life. It belongs within a wider Kurdish linguistic landscape whose varieties and communities must be distinguished. A restriction documented for Kurmanji in Turkey cannot automatically be retold as the experience of Sorani speakers in Iraq or Iran. Shared identity does not make every legal history identical.

Conflict, displacement, and political struggles have repeatedly shaped Kurdish public life. At the same time, Sorani has developed institutions, literature, education, and media. The honest account holds both realities together. This page does not describe Sorani as a language that disappeared and was later recreated, nor assign every Kurdish community the same level or form of endangerment.

sections.heading: Official status changes the possibilities for public use
paragraphs: Article 4 of Iraq’s 2005 Constitution makes Arabic and Kurdish the country’s official languages. It addresses education and official communication as well as the rights of other language communities. This is a major legal milestone for Kurdish, but the constitutional category is Kurdish broadly; it should not be paraphrased as a law concerning Sorani alone.

National recognition also has geographic limits. Iraq’s Constitution does not determine the rights of speakers in Iran or every diaspora setting. Even within a country, the existence of a right and the practical ability to use it are separate questions. A language history should identify which jurisdiction a law governs before presenting it as protection available to a particular reader.

sections.heading: A language survives through ordinary public usefulness
paragraphs: In February 2023, the Kurdistan Regional Government announced measures concerning Kurdish learning for foreign residents and Kurdish-language signage, menus, guides, and instructions. The announcement cited the region’s 2014 Official Languages Law. These measures illustrate an important part of language development: making the language available for practical public tasks, beyond celebration or ceremonial recognition.

Government announcements describe policy intentions; they are not independent proof that implementation is complete. For learners, education, publishing, broadcasting, and community organizations offer ways to encounter Sorani in use. Supporting those sources means checking who produced the material, which variety it represents, and how it fits the circumstances of the people who use it.

sections.heading: Right-to-left typing is part of the writing system
paragraphs: For Sorani practice, use an appropriate Kurdish keyboard and preserve distinctions such as ڕ, ڵ, ۆ, and ێ. Similar-looking Arabic or Persian characters can have different underlying code points. Our publication standard requires competent review of the text and explicit testing of right-to-left display, cursor behavior, and input composition before a passage is offered as a scored exercise.

Read the complete sentence first and check the meaning alongside a trusted source. A mismatch may involve spelling, a character substitution, or the input method, so examine the actual text before interpreting a low score. Standard five-character WPM describes mechanical performance; it cannot certify Kurdish proficiency, compare language difficulty, or judge a speaker’s cultural connection.

timeline: 20th century

sections.heading: A language pushed out of public life, not one that simply faded away
paragraphs: ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi was a language of government, newspapers, schooling, relationships, and intellectual life in the Hawaiian Kingdom. Its decline cannot honestly be presented as a natural change of preference. After the Kingdom’s overthrow in 1893, the Republic of Hawaiʻi’s 1896 education law required English as the medium and basis of instruction in public and private schools. Hawaiian could no longer occupy its former place as the language through which children received their education. The law did not ban every private conversation in Hawaiian; that distinction does not make its consequences small.

Language suppression also belongs within a wider history of attacks on cultural practice. Hawaiʻi’s Legislature records Kaʻahumanu’s prohibition of public hula performances under Christian influence, while recognizing that Hawaiians continued teaching and performing despite it. Specific prohibitions, institutional pressure, and continuing resistance must be named accurately. A claim that a single law prohibited all Hawaiian culture would flatten a complicated history and obscure the people who kept traditions alive.

sections.heading: School punishment, separation, and the damage to transmission
paragraphs: Schoolchildren did experience punishment for speaking Hawaiian. Elder recollections published through the University of Hawaiʻi describe being made to repeat a written prohibition on speaking the language. Such experiences could teach a child that the language of home brought humiliation at school. The University’s territorial-schooling archive also documents Native Hawaiian petitions and legislative proposals seeking language instruction and greater control of education. Families were not passive witnesses to suppression; they fought it through the institutions available to them.

Boarding and reformatory institutions require equally careful attention. A 2024 U.S. Senate report connects missionary boarding education in Hawaiʻi with assimilation through Christianity and labor. At Waialeʻe on Oʻahu, the community research project Nā Lei Poina ʻOle describes predominantly Native Hawaiian boys incarcerated for minor offenses, and the resulting trauma and indoctrination. Waialeʻe was a reformatory, not an ordinary school. These histories show separation and institutional harm; they do not establish that every institution, child, or punishment followed an identical pattern. No story of a fatal school fire is asserted here.

sections.heading: The emergency that families answered with immersion
paragraphs: By the early 1980s, transmission to young people had reached a crisis. In 2018 Senate testimony, Nāmaka Rawlins recalled the survey undertaken when ʻAha Pūnana Leo began in 1983: it identified 37 fluent speakers aged eighteen and under statewide. This is the organization’s reported historical count, not a current estimate or an interchangeable census measure. It conveys why advocates understood the situation as an emergency involving the next generation.

ʻAha Pūnana Leo’s community history places its founding in 1983 and the first preschool in Kekaha, Kauaʻi, in August 1984. The movement learned from Māori kōhanga reo and sought environments where Hawaiian was the ordinary language of interaction. Advocacy secured removal of the school restriction in 1986; public Kaiapuni classes followed at Keaukaha and Waiau in 1987. Rawlins describes parents learning, building teaching materials, maintaining classrooms, and raising funds. This was sustained labor by families and educators, not an effortless comeback following a policy announcement.

sections.heading: Official status did not finish the work
paragraphs: Hawaiian became an official state language in 1978, before the school restriction was removed. Recognition and daily opportunities to speak are different achievements. The Department of Education describes the growth of Kaiapuni alongside continuing shortages of qualified Hawaiian-speaking teachers and suitable facilities. Its account treats community leadership as central. Education has rebuilt a pathway for children, but maintaining that pathway demands people, resources, and institutional commitment.

OHA’s 2025 community-based study follows Hawaiian use across home, school, and community and identifies both successes and continuing needs in intergenerational engagement. It should not be mistaken for a statewide fluency census. There are fluent speakers and families who live through Hawaiian today; acknowledging them does not erase the rupture. Nor should discussion of lost knowledge imply that contemporary speakers use a language without depth. Smithsonian reporting on Hawaiian-medium hula shows practitioners carrying cultural knowledge while working to reconnect language, story, and practice.

sections.heading: Written practice should follow the people carrying the language
paragraphs: A typing exercise can provide a small place to practice written accuracy. It cannot repair historical harm, confer cultural belonging, or replace relationships with speakers and teachers. Preserve the ʻokina and kahakō, including ā, ē, ī, ō, and ū. Follow the spelling and context of a trusted source instead of removing marks to obtain a faster score. A mechanical WPM result is not a measure of fluency or understanding.

Begin with short, clearly attributed learning material and seek guidance where meanings or usage are uncertain. Culturally significant texts, including prayers, genealogy, and mele, should not be treated as interchangeable test filler. Support community-led education, listen as well as type, and make room for the language in ordinary life. The credit for survival and revitalization belongs to the kūpuna, families, teachers, advocates, and living communities doing that work.
